svg.title: Why summarization is the only real scalability lever in an L3VPN, and the three ways to apply it
svg.desc: Left panel: a scaling arithmetic. Eight hundred branches with four prefixes each is three thousand two hundred routes per VRF, so twenty VRFs is sixty four thousand VPN routes held by every PE and every route reflector. A summary reduces the branch contribution to a handful of prefixes, which multiplies out to a manageable number. Right panel lists the three places a summary can be applied: at the PE-CE boundary with a static route to null0, inside the VRF with an aggregate that is advertised into MP-BGP, and at the route reflector if it is used as a summarization point. Each row gives the benefit and the risk. A bottom note explains that the null0 route is what makes the summary safe, and that a summary without it becomes a black hole for any member prefix that disappears.
svg.text: Every PE and every reflector holds every route: that is the bill summarization reduces
The arithmetic is dull, and it is the only argument that survives a budget meeting
Without summarization
800 branches × 4 prefixes = 3 200 routes per VRF
20 VRFs × 3 200 = 64 000 VPNv4 routes
× every PE and every reflector that keeps a full table
Each additional site costs memory, update generation and
convergence time on devices that never see its traffic.
This is why an L3VPN that worked at 50 sites becomes
unmanageable at 500 without anyone changing the design.
With summary per region
800 branches → 20 regions × 1 summary = 20 routes
20 VRFs × 20 = 400 VPNv4 routes in the core
The detail stays at the regional PE, where it is needed.
Failure scope also shrinks: a branch going down changes
nothing in the core, because no core route depended on it.
Cost: the summary is now the unit of reachability, so a
regional mistake hides a whole region from everyone else.
THREE PLACES TO APPLY IT
1. At the PE-CE boundary: a static summary plus a discard route towards null0, redistributed into MP-BGP. Cheapest, most stable.
2. Inside the VRF toward MP-BGP: aggregate the customer's own prefixes and advertise only the aggregate. Keeps the customer's IGP untouched.
3. At the reflector: possible, but it makes the reflector a policy point and a single point of failure for reachability. Rarely worth it.
The null0 rule: a summary without a discard route is a promise about prefixes that may not exist. When one disappears, the summary keeps forwarding into a void.
Write the summary and the null0 route as one configuration item, so nobody can add one without the other.
